draft.title: Accrued expenses
card: An accrued expense is an expense that has been used or incurred in the period but has not yet been paid. Wages owing at balance day is a common example.
On balance day, the business records the expense, which reduces profit for the period. It also records a liability, such as accrued wages, for the amount owing.
The liability appears on the balance sheet at the end of the period, because the business owes the money.
In the next period, when the business pays, the payment clears the liability. It is not recorded as a new expense for that period.
draft.remember: Accrued expense: record the expense and a liability now, then clear the liability when paid.

a.q: On balance day a business owes employees for work done but has not paid them. What is recorded?
opts: A wages expense and a liability for wages owing
A wages expense and an asset for wages owing
A liability only, with no change to expenses
An asset only, with no change to expenses
a.why: The work was done this period, so the wages are an expense now. The business owes the money, so a liability is created. An asset is wrong because the business has not gained anything it owns.
a.clue: Does the business own the amount, or owe it?

b.q: Tariq owns a landscaping firm in Geelong. At 30 June he owes workers $1 200 for the last week of June, to be paid on 4 July. What happens when he pays on 4 July?
opts: The accrued wages liability is cleared
A new $1 200 wages expense is recorded for July
Accrued wages are recorded as revenue
The $1 200 is added to assets as a prepayment
b.why: The expense was already recorded in June, so the July payment clears the liability. Recording a new expense would count the same wages twice.
b.clue: The expense was recorded on balance day.

a.best: A wages expense and a liability for wages owing

b.best: The accrued wages liability is cleared
